items.prompt: What makes a decision a 'multi-criteria decision,' in this unit's sense?
choices: Several distinct, hard-to-compare factors all bear on which option is best, with no single number capturing all of them
Any decision that takes more than one meeting to resolve
A decision where exactly one factor is uncertain, like future cost
A decision made by more than one person
items.explanation: A multi-criteria decision isn't defined by how long it takes or how many people are involved -- it's defined by having several genuinely different factors (risk, cost, maintainability, etc.) that can't be collapsed into one another.
items.reference:
📏 several criteria, none reducible to the others
⚖️ weights say how much each one counts

Why: A multi-criteria decision has no single number that captures every factor -- naming the criteria and weighing them explicitly is what makes a structured comparison possible at all.

items.prompt: Priya, Marcus, and Dana are each arguing for a different priority (deploy velocity, operational risk, onboarding speed). Why does this count as a multi-criteria decision rather than three people just disagreeing about facts?
choices: Because each of them is prioritizing a genuinely different, non-interchangeable factor -- the disagreement is about weighting, not about what's true
Because they're arguing in the same meeting
Because none of them has read the roadmap
Because the decision hasn't been made in three weeks
items.explanation: None of them is factually wrong about their own priority mattering. The disagreement is about how much each factor should count relative to the others -- exactly the shape of a multi-criteria decision.
items.reference:
📏 several criteria, none reducible to the others
⚖️ weights say how much each one counts

Why: A multi-criteria decision has no single number that captures every factor -- naming the criteria and weighing them explicitly is what makes a structured comparison possible at all.

Calculating the expected dollar cost of a vendor's usage-based pricing tier
Predicting whether a coin flip lands heads
items.explanation: Build-vs-buy genuinely involves several incommensurable factors at once. The other options are single-dimension questions with one uncertain number attached -- the kind of problem expected-value tools handle.
items.reference:

⚖️ weights say how much each one counts

Why: A multi-criteria decision has no single number that captures every factor -- naming the criteria and weighing them explicitly is what makes a structured comparison possible at all.

items.prompt: What does it mean for two criteria to be 'incommensurable,' as used in this unit?
choices: They can't be converted onto a common scale -- operational risk isn't 'worth' some exact number of onboarding-weeks
They're both equally important by definition
One of them must be a mistake, since real criteria always reduce to cost
They can never both be scored on a 1-10 scale
items.explanation: Incommensurable criteria are genuinely different kinds of things -- there's no exchange rate between operational risk and onboarding speed the way there is between two amounts of money. That's why they need weights, not a conversion formula.
items.reference:
📏 several criteria, none reducible to the others
⚖️ weights say how much each one counts

Why: A multi-criteria decision has no single number that captures every factor -- naming the criteria and weighing them explicitly is what makes a structured comparison possible at all.

items.prompt: How does this unit's problem (multiple competing criteria) differ from the problem `expected-value` covers (one criterion under uncertainty)?
choices: expected-value handles uncertainty about one dimension's outcome (like cost); this unit handles combining several genuinely different dimensions that don't reduce to each other
They're the same problem with different names
expected-value only applies to financial decisions and this unit only applies to technical ones
This unit is just expected-value applied three times in a row
items.explanation: expected-value is about probability-weighting the possible outcomes of a single dimension. This unit is about weighing several different dimensions -- cost, risk, maintainability -- none of which collapse into a single probability-weighted number.
items.reference:
📏 several criteria, none reducible to the others
⚖️ weights say how much each one counts

Why: A multi-criteria decision has no single number that captures every factor -- naming the criteria and weighing them explicitly is what makes a structured comparison possible at all.

items.prompt: A teammate says 'let's just convert operational risk into a dollar cost and add it to the budget, then it's a single-number decision.' What's the issue with that move?
choices: It's sometimes possible with real effort, but often forces a fake precision onto a factor that was never truly a dollar amount -- collapsing incommensurable criteria doesn't remove the judgment call, it hides it
It's always the correct and only valid approach to any multi-criteria decision
Operational risk can never be expressed in any numeric form under any circumstances
This is exactly what a weighted-scoring matrix does, so there's no difference
items.explanation: Forcing every criterion into one unit doesn't eliminate the underlying judgment call about how much risk 'costs' -- it just buries that judgment call inside a conversion rate instead of keeping it visible as an explicit weight.
items.reference:
📏 several criteria, none reducible to the others
⚖️ weights say how much each one counts

Why: A multi-criteria decision has no single number that captures every factor -- naming the criteria and weighing them explicitly is what makes a structured comparison possible at all.

items.prompt: What is a 'weight,' as this unit uses the term?
choices: A number expressing how much a given criterion should count relative to the others, made explicit rather than left as an unstated personal priority
The raw 1-10 score an option gets on one criterion
The total number of criteria in the decision
A synonym for 'the correct answer'
items.explanation: A weight isn't a score for an option -- it's how much a criterion counts, period, regardless of which option is being evaluated. Scores and weights are different numbers doing different jobs.
items.reference:
🤷 unstated priorities look like disagreement about the decision
📝 named priorities look like disagreement about one weight

Why: Writing criteria and weights down turns a shapeless argument into a specific, resolvable disagreement about a single number.

items.prompt: Before the fourth meeting in L1's scenario, were Priya, Marcus, and Dana implicitly using weights at all?
choices: Yes -- each was privately weighting one factor above the others, they just hadn't said so, which is exactly what made the argument unresolvable
No -- weights only exist once they're written on a whiteboard
No -- they were each arguing from pure fact with no judgment involved
Yes, but only Marcus had a real priority; the others were just being difficult
items.explanation: Each of them already had an implicit weighting in their head -- the problem wasn't the absence of weights, it was that the weights were silent and unstated, so the group was arguing about the conclusion instead of the actual point of disagreement.
items.reference:

📝 named priorities look like disagreement about one weight

Why: Writing criteria and weights down turns a shapeless argument into a specific, resolvable disagreement about a single number.

items.explanation: No new facts were introduced. What changed was making each person's implicit priority explicit and written down, which turned a shapeless disagreement into a specific, resolvable one about a single weight.

items.prompt: What is 'sensitivity analysis,' in the context of a multi-criteria decision?
choices: Re-checking whether a decision's top-scoring option still wins under other reasonable weightings, instead of trusting the first one tried
A survey asking employees how they feel about a decision
A one-time calculation that never needs to be repeated once the first weighting is chosen
A synonym for 'weight' used interchangeably in this unit
items.explanation: Sensitivity analysis is specifically about testing robustness -- rerunning the scoring under several plausible weightings to see whether the same option keeps winning, or whether the first result was fragile.
items.reference:
🔁 rerun scoring under 2-4 other plausible weightings
🏆 same winner every time -> robust
🔀 winner flips -> the number was one guess, not a signal

Why: A recommendation built on only the first weighting anyone tried is trusting one person’s judgment call more than it deserves.

items.prompt: What does 'tie-breaker judgment' mean in this unit, and when does it apply?
choices: Deciding on factors like reversibility or who bears the cost of being wrong, used when two options score too close together for the numeric gap to be a reliable signal
Flipping a coin whenever two options are close
Always deferring to whoever has the most seniority in the room
A step that replaces the weighted-scoring matrix entirely, used instead of it from the start
items.explanation: Tie-breaker judgment is specifically for the close-call case -- when the score gap is thin enough that it isn't a trustworthy signal, the decision should turn on reversibility, who bears the cost, or what would be regretted more, not on squeezing more precision from noisy inputs.
items.reference:
🔁 rerun scoring under 2-4 other plausible weightings
🏆 same winner every time -> robust
🔀 winner flips -> the number was one guess, not a signal

Why: A recommendation built on only the first weighting anyone tried is trusting one person’s judgment call more than it deserves.

items.prompt: In the weighted-scoring matrix mechanic, what are the three steps in order?
choices: List options and assign criteria weights, score every option per criterion, compute each option's weighted score (sum of score x weight)
Score every option first, then decide afterward what the criteria even are
Pick a winner by gut feeling, then build a matrix to justify it after the fact
Assign weights, then discard the criteria that scored lowest before doing any scoring
items.explanation: The order matters: criteria and weights are decided before scoring options, so the scoring isn't biased by already knowing which option a given weighting would favor.
items.reference:
1️⃣ list options and criteria, assign weights
2️⃣ score every option per criterion
3️⃣ weighted score = sum of (score × weight)

Why: The matrix combines several incommensurable criteria into one comparable number per option -- not a measurement, a structured combination of judgment calls.

items.prompt: In the matrix, why should the weights for all criteria sum to a fixed total, like 1.0?
choices: So 'how much this criterion counts' is comparable across criteria -- a weight of 0.30 only means something relative to the other weights summing with it
Because scores must always be whole numbers
It's an arbitrary convention with no effect on the result
So that every option automatically gets the same final score
items.explanation: A fixed total makes weights comparable to each other -- 0.30 out of 1.0 clearly means 'the largest single factor,' whereas an unconstrained set of weights loses that shared reference point.
items.reference:
1️⃣ list options and criteria, assign weights
2️⃣ score every option per criterion
3️⃣ weighted score = sum of (score × weight)

Why: The matrix combines several incommensurable criteria into one comparable number per option -- not a measurement, a structured combination of judgment calls.

items.prompt: Stay-monolith scores 8 on operational risk (weight 0.30) and 4 on maintainability (weight 0.20). What's its weighted contribution from just these two criteria?
items.explanation: Each criterion's contribution is its own score times its own weight, and the contributions are added -- not multiplied together, and not summed before weighting.
items.reference:
1️⃣ list options and criteria, assign weights
2️⃣ score every option per criterion
3️⃣ weighted score = sum of (score × weight)

Why: The matrix combines several incommensurable criteria into one comparable number per option -- not a measurement, a structured combination of judgment calls.

items.prompt: After a weighted matrix produces 7.6 vs. 5.55, what's true about those numbers no matter how carefully the arithmetic was checked?
choices: The weights and 1-10 scores feeding them are still someone's honest estimate, not a measurement -- careful arithmetic on subjective inputs still produces a subjective output
They are now objectively correct and can't reasonably be disputed
The arithmetic being correct guarantees the criteria list was complete
Once computed, weights no longer need to be reviewed for future decisions
items.explanation: Careful arithmetic doesn't upgrade the nature of its inputs. A weighted score is exactly as reliable as the honesty and care behind the weights and scores that produced it -- no more.
items.reference:
1️⃣ list options and criteria, assign weights
2️⃣ score every option per criterion
3️⃣ weighted score = sum of (score × weight)

Why: The matrix combines several incommensurable criteria into one comparable number per option -- not a measurement, a structured combination of judgment calls.

items.prompt: What's the actual value of building a weighted-scoring matrix, if its inputs are just estimates rather than measurements?
choices: It makes each judgment call explicit and inspectable -- so a disagreement can target one specific weight or score instead of staying a vague, unaddressable objection
It removes the need for any human judgment from the decision
It has no real value if the inputs aren't objective measurements
It guarantees the chosen option is the best possible one
items.explanation: The matrix's value isn't manufacturing objectivity -- it's converting vague disagreement into a specific, arguable claim about one number, which is exactly what let L1's stuck meeting resolve in twenty minutes.
items.reference:
1️⃣ list options and criteria, assign weights
2️⃣ score every option per criterion
3️⃣ weighted score = sum of (score × weight)

Why: The matrix combines several incommensurable criteria into one comparable number per option -- not a measurement, a structured combination of judgment calls.

items.prompt: Why rerun the weighted-scoring matrix under several different weightings instead of trusting the first one?
choices: Because the first weighting is just one person's judgment call, and checking whether the winner holds under other plausible weightings tests whether the recommendation is robust or fragile
Because the first weighting is always wrong by definition
Because more weightings always produce a higher-scoring winner
It's not actually useful -- the first weighting is sufficient once the arithmetic is checked
items.explanation: Sensitivity analysis exists specifically because a single weighting reflects one person's (or one meeting's) judgment call -- rerunning it under other plausible weightings is what distinguishes a robust recommendation from a fragile one.
items.reference:
🔁 rerun scoring under 2-4 other plausible weightings
🏆 same winner every time -> robust
🔀 winner flips -> the number was one guess, not a signal

Why: A recommendation built on only the first weighting anyone tried is trusting one person’s judgment call more than it deserves.

items.prompt: Marcus thinks operational risk deserves weight 0.40 instead of 0.30. Does his disagreement mean the original matrix was wasted effort?
choices: No -- the matrix already turned a vague objection into a specific, testable claim about one weight, which is exactly what sensitivity analysis is built to check
Yes -- any disagreement about a weight means the whole exercise has to be discarded and restarted from nothing
Yes, because a matrix is only useful if literally everyone agrees on every weight before it's built
No, but only because Marcus is wrong and should be overruled
items.explanation: A specific weight disagreement is progress, not failure -- it's now a testable claim ('does the winner change if risk gets more weight') instead of an unaddressable feeling that the decision is wrong.
items.reference:
🔁 rerun scoring under 2-4 other plausible weightings
🏆 same winner every time -> robust
🔀 winner flips -> the number was one guess, not a signal

Why: A recommendation built on only the first weighting anyone tried is trusting one person’s judgment call more than it deserves.

items.prompt: What should happen if a sensitivity check shows the same option winning comfortably under every plausible weighting tried?
choices: Treat the recommendation as robust -- the exact weights barely matter to the outcome, so the decision can be made with real confidence
Assume the check was performed incorrectly, since real decisions should always be close
Discard the result and default to whichever option is cheapest
Keep testing indefinitely, since no number of consistent results is ever enough
items.explanation: A winner that holds up across multiple plausible weightings is the strongest form of confidence this framework can produce -- that's the intended, useful outcome of running a sensitivity check, not a reason for more suspicion.
items.reference:

🏆 same winner every time -> robust
🔀 winner flips -> the number was one guess, not a signal

items.prompt: A weighted matrix produces a 2% score gap between the top two options. What should that thin margin change about how the decision gets made?
choices: The numeric gap shouldn't be trusted as the deciding factor -- something else, like reversibility or who bears the cost of being wrong, should decide instead
Nothing -- whichever option scored even slightly higher should always be chosen
The weights should be recomputed to more decimal places until the gap widens
The decision should be delayed indefinitely until the gap becomes larger
items.explanation: A margin that thin, built on 1-10 estimates, is noise rather than signal. Trusting it as a tiebreaker manufactures false confidence -- a different kind of question (reversibility, who bears the cost) should decide instead.
items.reference:
📏 a thin score gap (a couple percent) isn’t a real signal
⚖️ reversibility, who bears the cost, what you’d regret

Why: Squeezing more precision out of inputs that were never precise doesn’t settle a close call -- a different kind of question does.

items.prompt: Why doesn't computing weights and scores to more decimal places help resolve a thin-margin tie?
choices: Because the underlying weights and scores were never that precise to begin with -- more decimal places on a fundamentally fuzzy estimate doesn't make it less fuzzy
Because more decimal places are mathematically impossible to compute
Because it would always flip the winner to the other option
It does help -- more precision is always the correct response to a close call
items.explanation: Extra decimal places create an illusion of precision on inputs that were honest guesses in the first place. The false sense of exactness is worse than admitting the numbers are genuinely close.
items.reference:
📏 a thin score gap (a couple percent) isn’t a real signal
⚖️ reversibility, who bears the cost, what you’d regret

items.prompt: Which of these is a legitimate tie-breaker for a thin-margin multi-criteria decision, per this unit?
choices: Which option is easier to reverse if it turns out to be the wrong call
Whichever option was proposed first in the original meeting
Whichever option has the longer written justification document
Recomputing the same weights and scores a second time without changing anything
items.explanation: Reversibility is one of the concrete, non-numeric factors this unit points to for close calls -- along with who bears the cost of being wrong and what would be regretted more -- none of which a recount of the same fuzzy inputs can substitute for.

items.prompt: A sensitivity check shows the same option winning under three plausible reweightings. Is this the same kind of guarantee as a passing automated test?
choices: No -- it's strong evidence the recommendation is robust to reasonable weight disagreement, but the underlying scores are still estimates and the criteria list itself might be incomplete
Yes -- three consistent results is mathematically equivalent to a formal proof of correctness
No -- sensitivity checks are purely decorative and carry no evidentiary value at all
Yes, as long as all three weightings were chosen by the same person
items.explanation: A robust result under sensitivity checking is meaningful evidence, but it's bounded by what was actually tested -- it doesn't verify the scores are accurate or that no criterion was missed, the way a passing test verifies behavior over its exact inputs.
items.reference:
✅ robust = holds under plausible reweighting
❌ not the same as mathematically proven correct

Why: The scores feeding the matrix are still estimates -- surviving a sensitivity check is strong evidence, not a guarantee.

items.prompt: What's one thing a sensitivity check that only varies weights can never catch?
choices: A criterion that nobody thought to include in the list at all, or a raw score that's simply wrong
Whether the winning option's weighted score is higher than the runner-up's
Whether the weights summed to a fixed total like 1.0
Whether more than one weighting was actually tried
items.explanation: Varying weights only tests sensitivity to weighting disagreement. It says nothing about a missing criterion or a factually wrong raw score -- both are separate failure modes a weights-only sensitivity check can't surface.
items.reference:
✅ robust = holds under plausible reweighting
❌ not the same as mathematically proven correct

Why: The scores feeding the matrix are still estimates -- surviving a sensitivity check is strong evidence, not a guarantee.

items.prompt: In `weightedScore(option, weights)`, why does the reduce walk `Object.keys(weights)` rather than `Object.keys(option.scores)`?
choices: Because only criteria present in the weighting should contribute to the score -- if `option.scores` had an extra criterion with no weight, it should be ignored, not silently counted
There's no difference; either key set always produces the same result
Because `option.scores` is guaranteed to never have extra keys
Because iterating weights is faster at runtime than iterating scores
items.explanation: Walking the weights' keys means the function only accumulates contributions from criteria that were actually assigned a weight -- an unweighted score sitting in `option.scores` correctly contributes nothing.
items.reference:
🧮 weightedScore: sum of (score × weight) per criterion
📊 rankOptions: sorts options by that score, highest first

Why: Object.keys(weights).reduce(...) walks every criterion once, multiplying and accumulating -- the same arithmetic as the by-hand matrix in L2, just executable.

items.prompt: What does `rankOptions(options, weights)` return, and in what order?
choices: An array of { name, score } objects, sorted highest score first
A single number: the highest weighted score across all options
The name of the winning option only, with no scores attached
An array sorted alphabetically by option name, ignoring score
items.explanation: rankOptions maps every option to its { name, score } pair via weightedScore, then sorts descending by score -- so ranked[0] is always the current winner and ranked[1] the runner-up, which top2Gap depends on.
items.reference:
🧮 weightedScore: sum of (score × weight) per criterion
📊 rankOptions: sorts options by that score, highest first

Why: Object.keys(weights).reduce(...) walks every criterion once, multiplying and accumulating -- the same arithmetic as the by-hand matrix in L2, just executable.

items.prompt: If a weighting object's values summed to 1.3 instead of 1.0, would the winner picked by rankOptions necessarily change?
choices: Not necessarily -- every option's score is inflated by roughly the same proportion, so the relative ranking is usually preserved even though the absolute scores no longer mean what they should
Yes -- an incorrect weight total always flips the winner
No -- rankOptions automatically re-normalizes any weighting to sum to 1.0 before scoring
It would make every option tie exactly
items.explanation: Since every option's score gets scaled by roughly the same inflated total, the relative order is typically unaffected -- but the absolute score, and any comparison of margins across differently-normalized weightings, becomes meaningless.
items.reference:
🧮 weightedScore: sum of (score × weight) per criterion
📊 rankOptions: sorts options by that score, highest first

Why: Object.keys(weights).reduce(...) walks every criterion once, multiplying and accumulating -- the same arithmetic as the by-hand matrix in L2, just executable.

items.prompt: What does `sensitivityAnalysis(options, weightSets)` compute for each weight set, per the L3 implementation?

Only a boolean: whether the winner is the same as the very first weight set
The average score across every option, ignoring rank
A list of every option's raw 1-10 scores, unweighted
items.explanation: For each label/weights pair, it ranks the options and reports the winner plus the score gap between first and second place -- the gap is what lets you judge whether a result is comfortable or thin.

The four weightings contradicting each other proves the whole matrix approach is unreliable and should be abandoned

🔀 winner flips -> the number was one guess, not a signal

It proves the whole weighted-matrix approach doesn't work and should never be used again

items.prompt: A compliance requirement nobody had weighed at all surfaces three weeks into a multi-criteria decision. What's the correct way to incorporate it into the existing sensitivity analysis?
choices: Treat it as a reason to restart weighting from scratch, since every existing weight was implicitly calibrated against an incomplete criteria list, not patch the old weight sets with the new criterion bolted on
Add the new criterion to `options[].scores` only, leaving every existing weight set unchanged
Ignore it, since sensitivity analysis is only meant to handle weight disagreement, not new criteria
Give the new criterion a weight of 0 so it doesn't disturb any of the existing results
items.explanation: Every existing weight was chosen relative to the old, incomplete list of criteria -- silently adding a new criterion without redoing the weighting understates it unevenly across options, which is worse than admitting the whole weighting needs revisiting.
items.reference:
➕ new criterion mid-decision -> restart weighting, don’t patch old weight sets
🔢 disagreement about a raw score -> find better evidence, not more weightings

Why: A weight dispute and a score dispute are different kinds of disagreement, and conflating them is a common way this framework gets misused.

No, because scores can never legitimately be disputed once entered into the matrix
Yes, because scores and weights are interchangeable inputs to the same function
items.explanation: A weight dispute and a score dispute are different problems. sensitivityAnalysis as built only tests robustness to weight changes -- resolving a disagreement about the actual 1-10 score requires finding who has the stronger evidence, not running more weightings.
items.reference:
➕ new criterion mid-decision -> restart weighting, don’t patch old weight sets
🔢 disagreement about a raw score -> find better evidence, not more weightings

Why: A weight dispute and a score dispute are different kinds of disagreement, and conflating them is a common way this framework gets misused.

items.prompt: Complete `weightedScore(option, weights)`. It should return the sum, over every criterion key present in `weights`, of `option.scores[criterion] * weights[criterion]`.

tests.expr: expect(weightedScore({ scores: { operationalRisk: 8, teamFamiliarity: 9, maintainability: 4, timeToValue: 9, cost: 8 } }, { operationalRisk: 0.30, teamFamiliarity: 0.25, maintainability: 0.20, timeToValue: 0.15, cost: 0.10 })).toBe(7.6)

tests.description: a single-criterion weighting returns score times weight

items.explanation: Object.keys(weights) walks only the weighted criteria, and reduce accumulates score times weight for each one. Starting the accumulator at 0 means an empty weighting correctly contributes nothing.
items.reference:
🧮 weightedScore: sum of (score × weight) per criterion
📊 rankOptions: sorts options by that score, highest first

Why: Object.keys(weights).reduce(...) walks every criterion once, multiplying and accumulating -- the same arithmetic as the by-hand matrix in L2, just executable.

items.prompt: The starter `weightedScore` below has a bug: it multiplies every score by the *same* weight instead of that criterion's own weight. Fix it so each criterion uses its own weight from the `weights` object.

tests.expr: expect(weightedScore({ scores: { operationalRisk: 8, teamFamiliarity: 9, maintainability: 4, timeToValue: 9, cost: 8 } }, { operationalRisk: 0.30, teamFamiliarity: 0.25, maintainability: 0.20, timeToValue: 0.15, cost: 0.10 })).toBe(7.6)

expect(weightedScore({ scores: { operationalRisk: 5, teamFamiliarity: 5, maintainability: 9, timeToValue: 4, cost: 4 } }, { operationalRisk: 0.30, teamFamiliarity: 0.25, maintainability: 0.20, timeToValue: 0.15, cost: 0.10 })).toBe(5.55)

tests.description: differently-weighted criteria no longer collapse to the same contribution
tests.expr: expect(weightedScore({ scores: { a: 10, b: 0 } }, { a: 0.9, b: 0.1 })).toBe(9)

items.explanation: The bug used the first weight found for every criterion, which silently collapses a multi-criteria matrix into a single-weight one -- every criterion needs its own weights[criterion] lookup, not one shared value.

items.prompt: Complete `topTwoGap(options, weights)`. Using the already-available `weightedScore` function, rank the options by weighted score (highest first) and return the numeric gap between the 1st and 2nd place scores.

tests.description: baseline weighting: gap between stay-monolith and extract-now is 2.05
tests.expr: expect(topTwoGap([{ name: 'a', scores: { c: 8 } }, { name: 'b', scores: { c: 3 } }], { c: 1 })).toBe(5)

tests.description: a three-option field still compares only the top two
tests.expr: expect(topTwoGap([{ name: 'a', scores: { c: 10 } }, { name: 'b', scores: { c: 7 } }, { name: 'c', scores: { c: 1 } }], { c: 1 })).toBe(3)

tests.description: a tie produces a gap of 0
tests.expr: expect(topTwoGap([{ name: 'a', scores: { c: 5 } }, { name: 'b', scores: { c: 5 } }], { c: 1 })).toBe(0)

items.explanation: Mapping every option to its weighted score, sorting descending, and subtracting the second entry from the first gives exactly the top2Gap sensitivityAnalysis reports -- the number that separates a comfortable win from a thin, judgment-call-required one.
items.reference:
🔁 rerun scoring under 2-4 other plausible weightings
🏆 same winner every time -> robust
🔀 winner flips -> the number was one guess, not a signal

Why: A recommendation built on only the first weighting anyone tried is trusting one person’s judgment call more than it deserves.

items.prompt: Complete `winnerHoldsAcrossAll(options, weightSets)`. Given an array of `{ label, weights }` objects, return `true` if the same option wins under every weight set, `false` if the winner ever differs.

tests.description: same winner under two weight sets returns true
tests.expr: const opts = [{ name: 'a', scores: { c: 9, r: 1 } }, { name: 'b', scores: { c: 1, r: 1 } }]; expect(winnerHoldsAcrossAll(opts, [{ label: 'x', weights: { c: 1, r: 0 } }, { label: 'y', weights: { c: 0.9, r: 0.1 } }])).toBe(true)

tests.description: a flipped winner under one weight set returns false
tests.expr: const opts = [{ name: 'a', scores: { c: 9, r: 1 } }, { name: 'b', scores: { c: 1, r: 9 } }]; expect(winnerHoldsAcrossAll(opts, [{ label: 'x', weights: { c: 1, r: 0 } }, { label: 'y', weights: { c: 0, r: 1 } }])).toBe(false)

tests.description: a single weight set trivially holds
tests.expr: const opts = [{ name: 'a', scores: { c: 5 } }, { name: 'b', scores: { c: 2 } }]; expect(winnerHoldsAcrossAll(opts, [{ label: 'only', weights: { c: 1 } }])).toBe(true)

items.explanation: Collecting the winning name under every weight set and checking they're all equal to the first is exactly what 'robust under sensitivity analysis' means in code -- one flipped entry anywhere in the list makes the whole check false.
